prize_parts.citation: For the optical lattice clock, based on trapping many atoms at the magic wavelength where the light shift cancels, and its development to the 10^-18 level of precision

statement.case_for: My preferred configuration is unchanged from round 1: B001 alone, Katori and Ye. After the full exchange I find the case stronger, not just more popular, because the chair's summary shows that the objections are about wording and credit, not about the physics. The mechanism is simple and general: at the magic wavelength the differential light shift of the clock transition vanishes, so many atoms can be confined and interrogated at once without the Doppler and recoil shifts of free or single-ion systems. That is a different principle from the comb (2005) and from single-ion control (2012), and it is what brought the statistical gain that made 10^-18 reachable. The result is also understood, which matters to me: blackbody, collisional and lattice-induced shifts are quantitatively modelled, and independent laboratories reproduce and compare clocks. Checkable consequences already exist, namely millimetre-scale gravitational redshift, bounds on varying constants and dark-matter couplings. Katori proposed the scheme and made the first strontium lattice clock; Ye's group took it to record systematics, stability and many-body clock physics. Two names are a defensible and compact credit.
statement.case_against: The strongest remaining objection, which all eight of us raised, is that this may be read as a refinement of the 2005 and 2012 prizes. I do not think it is settled, and a citation that says only 'precision' would invite it; the citation must name the lattice and magic-wavelength principle. The second is credit: Lemonde, Ludlow, Bloom, Hinkley, Campbell and the Paris, NIST/Boulder and PTB groups made decisive steps, and a three-person cap cannot cover them; none of us, including me, has verified the exact priority record from primary sources. Third, whether to wait for the SI second redefinition. I see it as a metrological decision that follows the physics, but I admit I cannot show that waiting would be wrong. I have also dropped my own first choice B006: its hexatic evidence is system dependent and some melting transitions are first order, which is a real scientific limitation and not only a lack of support, and Olsson's point about experimental verification applies to it.

responses.point: Olsson asks whether the 10^-18 headline is a discovery about nature or a record in systematic control, and says the case depends on whether the magic-wavelength proposal and first lattice clock are the invention, rather than the later record accuracy.
responses.response: I think the answer is that the two cannot be separated, which is why the citation should carry both halves. The magic-wavelength idea is the invention; the 10^-18 level is the evidence that it works as a general mechanism, because it required understanding and cancelling every systematic shift to that depth. A record that is only a record would not have produced millimetre-scale redshift measurements or dark-matter bounds. I therefore support your framing that the prize is for the original scheme and its realisation, with the precision as the demonstration, and I have written my citation that way. I also accept your point that this protects the award better than an 'accuracy' citation against the 2005 and 2012 overlap.

responses.point: Johansson moved from B003 to B001 because colleagues with no stake in circuit QED converge on the clock, and lists B003 and B042 as alternatives; he also flags that it is outside his expertise to verify metrology priorities and that circuit QED follows the 2025 prize closely.
responses.response: I agree with your reasoning for setting B003 aside this year, and I respect that you flagged your own entanglement with that field and offered to recuse. On B042 I would be cautious about promoting it as a second part: the chair's summary shows no two proposals choose the same three of Bloch, Cirac, Greiner, Zoller and Esslinger, and the theory-versus-experiment split is exactly the kind of credit question that a three-person cap forces us to settle by taste. I would only add a second part if a single defensible slate emerges, and so far none has. Adding it now would dilute a clean two-name prize rather than improve it.

responses.point: Kroll notes the road from record uncertainty to broad scientific use is long, cannot claim the new-physics payoff is yet demonstrated, and asks whether a two-part prize adding B042 or B003 would improve the configuration or only dilute it.
responses.response: I take the caution about the payoff seriously, but I would separate demonstrated from anticipated. Time dilation over millimetres and bounds on varying constants and dark-matter couplings have already been obtained with these clocks, even if the largest application, the redefinition of the second, is still ahead. On your two-part question my answer is that I would not add one: the other candidates each carry an unresolved credit or maturity problem (five names in B042, four in B003 with a recusal and a recent circuit prize, an under-ten-year-old B017 whose pairing mechanism is open), and a weak second part would weaken the clock prize more than it would strengthen the configuration.

responses.point: Eriksson moved from B010 to B001 and still lists B010 as an alternative, with credit among Kane-Mele, Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang, Fu-Kane-Mele and Hasan genuinely split.
responses.response: We agree that the topological insulator credit cannot be represented by three names without deciding a priority dispute. I would add that it cannot be resolved by our deliberations alone either, and so I would not make a second part out of it this year. If the committee later wants to return to the field, the framing question between B010 (Kane, Mele, Molenkamp) and B004 (Kane, Molenkamp, Xue) must be answered first; I would not want to settle that under time pressure in a vote.

uncertainties: Whether the committee regards the lattice clock as a distinct achievement or as a continuation of the 2005 and 2012 prizes; I judge it distinct but have not shown it conclusively.

Priority record for the magic-wavelength proposal, the first strontium lattice clock and the 10^-18 results, which I have not verified from primary sources, and whether Lemonde, Ludlow, Bloom or other groups have claims strong enough to join or displace Katori and Ye.
Timing relative to the SI second redefinition, which I treat as following the physics.

For the alternatives, I rely on memory of the 2D melting literature for B006 and have not verified relative priority among Young, Halperin and Nelson, nor the extent to which first-order melting limits the hexatic scenario.
Whether a two-part prize would be wise if a defensible B042 slate emerged; I currently see none.
statement.conflict_note: No change from round 1. No specific conflict is apparent from my profile, and none of the credited persons on the shortlist is a frequent co-author or institutional colleague of mine. Gothenburg colleagues on the committee (Johansson, Olsson) work in neighbouring fields, with no collaboration with me that I know of. I note Johansson's disclosed conflict on B003, which is relevant only if that part were revived.
